title: Labor Watchdog: H-1B Was Meant to Be Temporary, Fraud Probe Now Criminal
excerpt: Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito told Fox News the visa was designed as short-term help, while warning employers under investigation that "we have handcuffs ready."
body:
• Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito told Fox News the H-1B program was created as temporary work authorization, not a permanent hiring channel — and says employers treating it otherwise face a criminal fraud probe.
  • His office launched a nationwide investigation into H-1B and PERM fraud in July 2026, has issued dozens of subpoenas, and executed search warrants at multiple locations.
  • D'Esposito warns the foreign-labor visa system will "look very different 365 days from now" — a warning, not an announced shutdown of the program.
  • What this means for you: investigators are targeting fake jobs, wage underpayment, worker "benching," sham employers and visa mills — not compliant petitions. If your employer is audited, keep LCA and payroll paperwork current, cooperate with site visits, and talk to counsel before answering questions you are unsure about. A separate H-1B restriction already runs through September 21, 2027.

The H-1B visa program was designed as temporary help for employers who could not find needed skills at home — and the department's top watchdog now says companies that built permanent staffing strategies around it are the target of a widening criminal investigation. Appearing on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show," Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito framed the crackdown as a return to the program's original design: foreign workers hired for defined periods while employers recruit Americans, not an evergreen pipeline.

"This is not a business model," D'Esposito said of the way employers use the program. His office is backing the rhetoric with investigative muscle: a nationwide probe into H-1B and PERM fraud opened in July 2026, "dozens" of subpoenas issued, and search warrants executed at multiple locations, according to VisaVerge's reporting on the probe.

Context & Background

The inspector general's office sits outside the Labor Department's chain of command and exists to investigate waste, fraud and abuse — which is why its involvement signals the issue has moved beyond paperwork disputes. D'Esposito, a former congressman from New York, has been telegraphing the shift in a series of X posts: "the H-1B fraud machine is being exposed" in September, followed by "Count your days," and later a sharper line — "H-1B fraud isn't a paperwork problem. It's a criminal one." In a separate video interview with commentator Benny Johnson, he said, "I think that the foreign labor visa program is going to look very different 365 days from now than it does today." He added, "We are building a case," and, "We have handcuffs ready."

Authorities are examining claims involving fake jobs, wage abuse, worker exploitation, sham employers, visa mills and wage kickbacks, VisaVerge reported. Earlier enforcement under "Project Firewall," launched in September 2025 under then–Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, already uncovered more than $15 million in back wages and documented benching, phantom worksites and wage underpayment across 175 active investigations.

Impact & Analysis

The watchdog's framing reframes the policy debate. The administration's critics have called the visa push a political assault on legal immigration; D'Esposito's case treats it as a labor-law enforcement action — employers who filed false labor condition applications, underpaid workers or benched them between assignments can already face back-pay orders, civil penalties and debarment of up to three years. Criminal referrals raise the stakes further for repeat offenders.

But the "temporary by design" argument cuts against how the program actually works for the workers themselves. H-1B visas run three years with a possible extension to six, and for Indian nationals — who face an 11-plus-year employment-based green-card backlog — the visa is often the only legal way to stay while waiting. In practice, the system has been a decades-long bridge, and D'Esposito's "look very different" warning leaves open how much of that bridge the administration intends to keep.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian professionals who hold roughly 71% of H-1B visas, the message is two-track: compliant workers at compliant employers have little to fear from a fraud probe, but the atmosphere is unsettled. Universities and hospitals that rely on H-1B and J-1 staff — including for physician residencies — are already fielding federal demands for workforce data, a sign the scrutiny extends beyond tech campuses.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

D'Esposito did not announce an abolition of the program; his formulation was change, not shutdown. Separately, President Trump extended restrictions on certain H-1B workers through September 21, 2027 — a fixed end date that stands apart from the inspector general's open-ended 365-day warning. The two tracks — criminal investigation and executive restriction — now converge on the next H-1B lottery cycle, when employers decide how many petitions to file, at what wage levels, and whether the paperwork risk is worth it. Arrests, if they come, will tell the market whether "handcuffs ready" was a metaphor or a plan.
